hello.title: Hello, Kotlin
hello.summary: Write your first Kotlin program with fun main and println, and print text and numbers.
hello.lesson.0: Every Kotlin program starts in a function called `main`. You write it as `fun main()`, followed by curly braces `{ }`. The code between the braces runs from top to bottom.
hello.lesson.2: `println` prints a value and then starts a new line. Text in double quotes, like `"Hello"`, is called a **string**. You do not need a semicolon at the end of a line.
hello.lesson.5: `print` prints without starting a new line. The next output continues on the same line. A `println` ends the line.
hello.lesson.8: Numbers do not need quotes. Kotlin calculates with `+`, `-`, `*` and `/`. It calculates the result first and then prints it. As in mathematics, `*` and `/` come before `+` and `-`, and parentheses come first.
hello.lesson.10: When you divide two whole numbers with `/`, Kotlin drops the rest: `7 / 2` is `3`. The operator `%` gives you the rest of a division. Write `7.0 / 2` to get `3.5`.
hello.lesson.12: `"5"` with quotes is a string, `5` without quotes is a number. For strings, `+` joins the text, so `"2" + "3"` is `23`.
hello.card.0: `fun main() { }` is where the program starts
hello.card.4: `"5"` is a string, `5` is a number
hello-1.prompt: Which line prints Hello and starts a new line?
hello-1.explain: `println` prints the value in the parentheses and then starts a new line.
hello-3.explain: `17 / 5` is `3` with a rest of `2`. The operator `%` gives the rest.
hello-4.options.0: `AB` and then `C` on the next line
hello-4.options.3: `A` and then `BC` on the next line
hello-4.explain: `print` does not start a new line, so `B` follows `A` directly. `println("B")` ends the line, and `C` comes on the next one.
hello-5.statement: `print` starts a new line after the output, like `println`.
hello-5.explain: Only `println` starts a new line. After `print`, the next output continues on the same line.
hello-6.prompt: Fill the gap so the program prints Hi.
hello-6.explain: Kotlin prints with `println` (or `print`). `echo`, `say` and `write` do not exist in Kotlin.
hello-7.prompt: Fill the gap so the program prints 3.5.
hello-7.explain: `7 / 2` divides two whole numbers and gives `3`. With `7.0` the result has a decimal part: `3.5`.
hello-8.prompt: Build a line that prints the result of 6 times 7.
hello-9.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program prints Kotlin on the first line and Done on the second.
hello-9.explain: `print("Kot")` stays on the line, `println("lin")` completes `Kotlin` and ends the line, then `Done` follows.
hello-10.prompt: Match the code with its meaning.
hello-10.pairs.0: prints and starts a new line
hello-11.explain: The string is not closed. Write `println("Middle")` with a closing quote.
hello-12.explain: Kotlin is case-sensitive. `Println` does not exist; write `println` with a small `p`.
variables.title: val, var and types
variables.summary: Store values with val and var, and meet the types Int, Double, String and Boolean.
variables.lesson.0: A **variable** is a name for a value. You create one with `val`, a name, `=` and a value. After that, you can use the name instead of the value.
variables.lesson.2: A `val` can never get a new value. If you need a value that changes, use `var`. You give it a new value with `=` again.
variables.lesson.4: Giving a `val` a new value is an error, and the program does not compile. Use `val` by default, and `var` only when the value must change.
variables.lesson.6: Every value has a **type**. `Int` is a whole number, `Double` is a number with a decimal point, `String` is text and `Boolean` is `true` or `false`. Kotlin finds the type from the value. This is called **type inference**.
variables.lesson.8: You can also write the type yourself, after the name and a colon: `val count: Int = 3`. A variable keeps its type: an `Int` variable can never hold a string. When you multiply an `Int` by a `Double`, the result is a `Double`.
variables.lesson.10: Short forms change a `var` in place: `x += 2` means `x = x + 2`, and `x -= 2` means `x = x - 2`. `x++` adds `1` and `x--` subtracts `1`.
variables.lesson.12: To turn a value into another type, use functions like `toDouble()`, `toInt()` and `toString()`. `toInt()` on a `Double` drops the decimal part. `toInt()` on a string like `"42"` gives the number `42`.
variables-1.prompt: Which keyword creates a variable that can get a new value later?
variables-1.explain: A `var` can change. A `val` keeps its first value forever.
variables-3.explain: An `Int` times a `Double` gives a `Double`, so the result is `6.0`, not `6`.
variables-4.statement: `val city = "Rome"` gives `city` the type `String`, even though no type is written.
variables-4.explain: Kotlin infers the type from the value. A value in double quotes is a `String`.
variables-5.prompt: Fill the gap so the program compiles and prints 11.
variables-5.explain: `total++` changes the variable, so it must be a `var`. A `val` cannot change.
variables-6.prompt: Fill the gap with the right type.
variables-6.explain: `1.75` has a decimal point, so its type is `Double`.
variables-7.prompt: Build a line that creates a variable age of type Int with the value 30.
variables-7.explain: The type comes after the name and a colon: `val age: Int = 30`. `"30"` would be a string.
variables-8.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program prints 8.
variables-8.explain: First create `n`, then add `5` to it, and print it at the end: `3 + 5 = 8`.
variables-9.prompt: Match each type with the values it holds.
variables-10.explain: `"25"` is a string, but `age` has the type `Int`. Write `val age: Int = 25` without quotes.
variables-11.explain: A `Double` cannot go into an `Int` variable. Convert it first: `val back: Int = double.toInt()`.
variables-12.explain: `a` and `b` are both `Int`, so `/` drops the rest: `10 / 4` is `2`.
strings.title: Strings and templates
strings.summary: Build text with string templates and work with length, uppercase() and substring().
strings.lesson.0: You can join strings with `+`. Kotlin also has a shorter way: a **string template**. Write `$` and a variable name inside a string, and Kotlin puts in the value.
strings.lesson.2: For a calculation or anything longer than a name, use curly braces: `${a + b}`. Kotlin runs the code inside the braces and puts the result into the string.
strings.lesson.5: `length` tells you how many characters a string has. Spaces count too. `uppercase()` and `lowercase()` return the string in capital or small letters.
strings.lesson.7: The characters are numbered from `0`, so `word[0]` is the first character. `substring(start, end)` returns the part from `start` up to `end`, without `end`. With only `start`, it goes to the end of the string.
strings.lesson.9: Because `end` is not included, `substring(1, 4)` has `4 - 1 = 3` characters.
strings.lesson.11: Strings have many more functions. `trim()` removes spaces at both ends, `contains` checks for a part, `replace` swaps text and `reversed()` turns the string around.
strings.lesson.13: A string never changes. Functions like `uppercase()` return a **new** string. To keep the result, store it in a variable: `val loud = word.uppercase()`.
strings.card.0: `"Hi, $name"` puts a value into a string
strings.card.1: `"${a + b}"` puts in the result of code
strings-1.explain: `$city` inside the string is replaced by the value of `city`.
strings-3.explain: Index `1` is `o`. The part goes up to index `4` without it: `o`, `t`, `l`.
strings-4.explain: `$a` and `$b` become `2` and `3`. `${a + b}` runs the calculation and becomes `5`.
strings-5.explain: `uppercase()` returns a new string, and the program does not store it. `word` is still `hello`.
strings-6.prompt: Fill the gap so the program prints Hi, Lea!
strings-6.explain: A string template starts with `$`: `"Hi, $name!"`. Without `$`, Kotlin prints the word `name`.
strings-7.prompt: Fill the gap so the program prints 7.
strings-7.explain: `length` is a property, so you write it without parentheses: `text.length`.
strings-8.prompt: Build a line that prints Name: and then the name in capital letters.
strings-8.explain: A function call inside a template needs curly braces: `${name.uppercase()}`. Without braces, only `$name` is replaced.
strings-9.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program prints KOTLIN has 6 letters.
strings-9.explain: You need `word` before you can make `loud` from it, and both before the `println`.
strings-10.prompt: Match the code with what it gives you.
strings-11.prompt: The program should print the number of letters in the first name. Which line has the bug?
strings-11.explain: Without `$`, the braces are printed as normal text. Write `${first.length}`.
strings-12.explain: `length` is a property, not a function. Write `word.length` without parentheses.
conditions.title: Decisions
conditions.summary: Make decisions with if, else and when, and combine comparisons with &&, || and !.
conditions.lesson.0: A comparison gives a `Boolean`: `true` or `false`. Kotlin has `==` (equal), `!=` (not equal), `<` (less than), `>` (greater than), `<=` and `>=`.
conditions.lesson.2: `if` runs a block of code only when a condition is `true`. The condition goes in parentheses. The `else` block is optional: it runs when the condition is `false`.
conditions.lesson.4: With `else if` you can check more conditions, one after the other. Kotlin runs the first block whose condition is `true` and skips the rest.
conditions.lesson.7: In Kotlin, `if` also gives back a value. You can store this value in a variable. In this case, the `else` part is required, because the variable needs a value in every case.
conditions.lesson.10: `when` compares one value with many options. Each branch has a value, an arrow `->` and a result. Several values can share a branch, separated by commas. `else` handles all other values. Like `if`, `when` can give back a value.
conditions.lesson.12: Without a value after `when`, every branch has its own condition, and the first true one wins. To combine conditions, use **logical operators**: `&&` (and) is `true` when both sides are true, `||` (or) when at least one side is true, and `!` (not) turns `true` into `false`.
conditions.card.2: `val max = if (a > b) a else b`
conditions-1.explain: `7 > 5` is `true`, so the first block runs.
conditions-2.explain: `9 % 2` is `1`, not `0`. The condition is `false`, so `if` gives back `"odd"`.
conditions-3.explain: The branch `2, 3` matches both `2` and `3`, so `text` is `"few"`.
conditions-4.explain: `!=` means "not equal". `5` is equal to `5`, so the result is `false`.
conditions-5.explain: `a > 2` is `true`, but `b < 5` is `false`. With `&&`, both sides must be true, so it prints `false`.
conditions-6.prompt: Fill the gap so that both conditions must be true to get in.
conditions-6.explain: `&&` needs both sides to be true. With `||`, the member would get in although `age` is only `15`.
conditions-7.prompt: Fill the gap so the program prints large.
conditions-7.explain: `if (condition) a else b` gives back `a` or `b`. Here `n > 10` is `true`, so `size` is `"large"`.
conditions-8.prompt: Build a line that stores the smaller of a and b in min.
conditions-8.explain: `if (a < b) a else b` gives back `a` when it is smaller, otherwise `b`.
conditions-9.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program prints Grade B.
conditions-9.explain: `75 >= 90` is `false`, so the `else` block runs. It must contain `println("Grade B")`.
conditions-10.prompt: Match each operator with its meaning.
conditions-10.pairs.1: or: at least one must be true
conditions-11.explain: A single `=` gives a variable a value. To compare, write `==`: `if (age == 18)`.
conditions-12.explain: When `if` gives a value to a variable, it needs an `else`: `if (points > 10) 5 else 0`.
loops.title: Loops and ranges
loops.summary: Repeat code with for loops over ranges like 1..5, until, step and downTo, and with while loops.
loops.lesson.0: A **range** is a sequence of numbers. `1..5` means `1`, `2`, `3`, `4`, `5`: both ends are included. A `for` loop runs its block once for every number in the range. The variable `i` holds the current number.
loops.lesson.2: `until` leaves out the end: `0 until 3` means `0`, `1`, `2`. You can also write it as `0..<3`. This is useful when you count from `0`.
loops.lesson.3: `step` jumps by more than one: `1..9 step 4` means `1`, `5`, `9`. `downTo` counts backwards: `3 downTo 1` means `3`, `2`, `1`. You can combine them.
loops.lesson.5: A loop often updates a variable. Here `sum` starts at `0`, and every round adds the current number to it.
loops.lesson.7: A `for` loop also works with a string. It goes through the characters one by one.
loops.lesson.10: A `while` loop repeats as long as its condition is `true`. It checks the condition before every round. Make sure that the condition becomes `false` at some point, or the loop never ends.
loops.lesson.12: `continue` skips the rest of the current round and goes on with the next one. `break` stops the whole loop at once.
loops-2.explain: `i` takes the values `0`, `3`, `6` and `9`. `10` is not included, so the loop runs four times.
loops-3.explain: `x` becomes `50`, `25`, `12` and then `6`. Now `x > 10` is `false`, and the loop stops.
loops-4.explain: `downTo` counts backwards from `5`, and `step 2` skips every second number: `5`, `3`, `1`.
loops-5.prompt: Which range contains exactly the numbers 0, 1, 2 and 3?
loops-5.explain: `..` includes both ends. `0 until 3` stops before `3`.
loops-6.statement: A `while` loop always runs its block at least once.
loops-6.explain: `while` checks the condition first. If it is `false` from the start, the block never runs.
loops-7.prompt: Fill the gap so the program prints 3, 2 and 1 on separate lines.
loops-7.explain: `3 downTo 1` counts backwards. `3..1` is an empty range, so the loop would print nothing.
loops-8.prompt: Fill the gap so the program prints 0, 2, 4, 6 and 8.
loops-9.prompt: Build the first line of a loop that counts from 1 to 10.
loops-9.explain: `for (i in 1..10) {` runs the block for every number from `1` to `10`. `1 until 10` would stop at `9`.
loops-10.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program prints 2, 4 and 6.
loops-10.explain: Print `n` first and then add `2`. In the other order, the program would print `4`, `6` and `8`.
loops-11.prompt: Match each range with its numbers.
loops-12.prompt: The program should print the sum of 1 to 10, which is 55. Which line has the bug?
loops-12.explain: `1 until 10` stops at `9`, so the sum is `45`. Write `1..10` to include `10`.
functions.title: Functions
functions.summary: Write your own functions with parameters, return types, default values and named arguments.
functions.lesson.0: A **function** is a block of code with a name. You can run it again and again. You define it with `fun`, a name, parentheses and a block. You call it with its name and `()`.
functions.lesson.2: **Parameters** pass values into a function. Each parameter has a name and a type, like `name: String`. When you call the function, you pass the values in the same order.
functions.lesson.4: A function can give back a result with `return`. Write the type of the result after the parentheses, like `: Int`. The caller can use the result like any other value.
functions.lesson.7: When a function only returns one expression, you can write it with `=`. Then you leave out the braces and `return`. Kotlin can infer the return type.
functions.lesson.10: A parameter can have a **default value**, like `greeting: String = "Hello"`. If the caller leaves it out, Kotlin uses the default value.
functions.lesson.12: With **named arguments**, you write the parameter name in the call, like `price = 3.5`. This makes calls easier to read. You can also skip a parameter with a default value, and you can pass the arguments in any order.
functions.card.1: `fun add(a: Int, b: Int): Int { return a + b }`
functions-2.explain: The call leaves out `age`, so the default value `30` is used.
functions-3.explain: `height` has the default value `2`, so `area(5)` is `5 * 2 = 10`.
functions-4.prompt: Which line correctly defines a function that returns an `Int`?
functions-4.explain: The return type comes after a colon, and every parameter needs a type. A block body needs `return`.
functions-5.statement: With named arguments, you can pass the arguments in a different order than the parameters.
functions-5.explain: Kotlin matches named arguments by their names, so `info(age = 7, name = "Tim")` works.
functions-6.prompt: Fill the gap so the function returns the sum.
functions-6.explain: `return` gives the value back to the caller. A function with the type `: Int` must return an `Int`.
functions-7.prompt: Fill the gap so the program prints Hi, Max!
functions-7.explain: `"Max"` goes to the first parameter, `name`, and `greeting` keeps its default value `"Hi"`.
functions-8.prompt: Build a single-expression function half that returns half of x.
functions-8.explain: A single-expression function uses `=` instead of a block: `fun half(x: Double) = x / 2`.
functions-9.prompt: Put the lines in order to build a function that returns the larger number.
functions-9.explain: If `a` is larger, the function returns `a` right away. Otherwise it goes on and returns `b`.
functions-10.prompt: Match the code with its meaning.
functions-10.pairs.1: gives back the value of x
functions-10.pairs.3: the body of a single-expression function
functions-11.explain: `average` needs two arguments and has no default values. Pass both, like `average(5, 6)`.
functions-12.explain: `isAdult` returns a `Boolean`, not an `Int`. Write `val ok: Boolean = isAdult(20)`.
collections.title: Lists, sets and maps
collections.summary: Store many values in lists, sets and maps, and transform lists with map and filter.
collections.lesson.0: A **list** holds many values in a fixed order. You create one with `listOf`. Indexes start at `0`, so `fruits[0]` is the first element. `size` tells you how many elements there are, and the last index is `size - 1`.
collections.lesson.2: A list from `listOf` cannot change. If you want to add, remove or replace elements, create it with `mutableListOf`.
collections.lesson.4: A `for` loop goes through every element of a list, in order. Lists also have ready-made functions like `sum()`, `max()` and `sorted()`.
collections.lesson.7: `map` creates a new list by changing every element. `filter` creates a new list with only the elements that match a condition. Inside the braces, `it` stands for the current element.
collections.lesson.10: A **set** stores every value only once, so duplicates are ignored. Use `setOf`, or `mutableSetOf` for a set that can change. The operator `in` checks if a value is in a collection.
collections.lesson.12: A **map** stores pairs of a key and a value. You create a pair with `to`. `ages["Ben"]` gives you the value for the key `"Ben"`. A `for` loop with `(name, age)` goes through all pairs.
collections-1.explain: Indexes start at `0`: `nums[0]` is `4`, `nums[1]` is `7` and `nums[2]` is `1`.
collections-2.explain: `map` gives the lengths `[3, 4, 4]`, and their sum is `11`.
collections-3.explain: A set keeps every value only once. Only `1`, `2` and `3` are left.
collections-4.explain: `filter` keeps only the elements for which `it > 3` is `true`.
collections-5.prompt: Which collection lets you add elements later?
collections-5.explain: Only the `mutable…` collections can change. `listOf`, `setOf` and `mapOf` are read-only.
collections-6.explain: `m["b"]` gives the value of the key `"b"`, which is `2`.
collections-7.prompt: Fill the gap so the program prints [1, 4, 9].
collections-7.explain: `map` changes every element: each number is multiplied by itself.
collections-8.prompt: Fill the gap so the program prints 3.
collections-8.explain: A map is accessed by its key, here the string `"tea"`. Maps do not use indexes like `0`.
collections-9.prompt: Build a line that keeps only the even numbers of nums.
collections-9.explain: `filter` keeps the elements that match the condition. `it % 2 == 0` is `true` for even numbers.
collections-10.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program prints [10, 20, 30].
collections-10.explain: Add `3` before you call `map`. Otherwise `big` is only `[10, 20]`.
collections-11.prompt: Match each collection with its description.
collections-12.prompt: The program should print the last name. Which line has the bug?
collections-12.explain: The indexes are `0` to `size - 1`. `names[3]` does not exist. Write `names[names.size - 1]`.
classes.title: Classes and null safety
classes.summary: Create your own types with class and data class, and handle missing values safely with ?, ?., ?: and !!.
classes.lesson.0: A **class** describes your own type. Its properties go into the parentheses after the class name: `val` for a property that never changes, `var` for one that can change. You create an **object** by calling the class like a function.
classes.lesson.2: A function inside a class is called a **method**. It can use the properties of the object. You call it with a dot, like `room.area()`.
classes.lesson.5: A `data class` is a class for holding data. Kotlin adds useful features: `println` shows the values, `==` compares the values, and `copy` creates a copy with some values changed. For a normal class, `==` only checks if both names point to the same object.
classes.lesson.8: `null` means "no value". In Kotlin, a normal type like `String` can never be `null`. If a variable may have no value, add a question mark to the type: `String?` is a **nullable** type.
classes.lesson.10: You cannot write `b.length` when `b` is nullable. The **safe call** `?.` gives `null` instead of an error when the value is `null`. The **Elvis operator** `?:` gives a default value when the left side is `null`.
classes.lesson.12: `!!` tells Kotlin: "I am sure that this is not `null`." If the value is `null` anyway, the program stops with a `NullPointerException`. Use `?.` and `?:` when you can.
classes.card.0: `class Dog(val name: String)`, `Dog("Rex")` creates an object
classes-1.explain: A data class prints its name and all its properties with their values.
classes-2.explain: `text` is `null`, so `text?.length` is `null`, and `?:` uses the default value `-1`.
classes-3.explain: The method `area` uses the properties of the object: `2 * 5 = 10`.
classes-4.explain: For a data class, `==` compares the values. Both objects have the same name, so the result is `true`.
classes-5.explain: Only a nullable type with `?`, like `String?`, can hold `null`.
classes-6.explain: `Cat` is a normal class, so `==` checks if `a` and `b` are the same object. They are two different objects.
classes-7.prompt: Fill the gap so the program prints 0.
classes-7.explain: The Elvis operator `?:` gives the default value `0` when the left side is `null`.
classes-8.prompt: Fill the gap so you can read the property name from outside.
classes-8.explain: `val` in the parentheses makes `name` a property. Without it, `name` is only a parameter, and `u.name` does not exist.
classes-9.prompt: Build a line that creates a copy of p in which y is 0.
classes-9.explain: `copy` creates a new object. With the named argument `y = 0`, only `y` changes.
classes-10.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program prints none and then ZOE.
classes-10.explain: While `name` is `null`, `?:` gives `none`. After `name = "Zoe"`, the safe call gives `ZOE`.
classes-11.prompt: Match the code with its meaning.
classes-11.pairs.3: stops the program if the value is null
classes-12.explain: `city` may be `null`, so `city.length` does not compile. Write `city?.length ?: 0`.
